questions.stem: What is the difference between an open system and a closed system?
options: An open system exchanges matter and energy with its surroundings; a closed system exchanges only energy
An open system exchanges only energy with its surroundings; a closed system exchanges matter and energy
An open system is always at equilibrium; a closed system can never reach equilibrium
An open system contains only gases; a closed system contains only liquids and solids
questions.explanation: In an open beaker, gases can escape, so matter leaves; a sealed flask lets heat in or out but keeps matter in. Equilibrium can only be established in a closed system.

questions.stem: Which statement about the reversibility of physical and chemical changes is correct?
options: No chemical reaction is reversible once its products have formed
Only reactions that absorb heat can ever be reversed in a closed system
Physical changes are generally reversible, but only some reactions are
All chemical reactions are reversible, but only some physical changes are
questions.explanation: Melting, boiling and dissolving can all be reversed. Some reactions, such as the formation of ammonia, are readily reversible, but others, such as combustion, are not reversible in practice.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate is heated in an open crucible and decomposes completely to calcium oxide. In a sealed container it does not. Why?
options: In the sealed container the reaction is slower, so it never reaches completion
In the sealed container the calcium oxide escapes, so no more can form
In the open crucible CO₂ escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot occur
In the open crucible oxygen enters, which reacts with the calcium carbonate
questions.explanation: CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g). In an open system the CO₂ is lost, so products cannot recombine and decomposition goes to completion. In a closed container CO₂ builds up and an equilibrium is set up.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a system at dynamic equilibrium?
options: The forward and reverse reactions have both stopped
The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
The forward reaction is faster than the reverse reaction
The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates
questions.explanation: At equilibrium both reactions keep going, but at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant. The concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.

questions.stem: A sealed bottle half full of water is left at constant temperature. After a while the water level stops falling. What is happening at the molecular level?
options: Molecules evaporate and condense at equal rates, so the level stays constant
Molecules have stopped evaporating, because the air above the water is full
Molecules evaporate only from the bottom of the bottle, where it is warmest
Molecules condense faster than they evaporate, so the vapour slowly disappears
questions.explanation: This is a physical equilibrium: evaporation continues, but condensation occurs at the same rate. The level is constant because the two processes balance, not because they stop.

questions.stem: A saturated solution of copper(II) sulfate contains some undissolved crystals. Radioactively labelled crystals are added. Later, labelled copper ions are found in solution. What does this show?
options: Equilibrium was disturbed, so all the crystals will eventually dissolve
Dissolving and crystallising go on at equal rates; the equilibrium is dynamic
The solution was not saturated, so the new crystals simply dissolved in it
The labelled crystals reacted with water to form a new copper compound
questions.explanation: Although the amount of solid does not change, ions continually leave the crystals and others are deposited. Labelled ions appear in solution because the exchange never stops.

questions.stem: What is meant by the position of an equilibrium?
options: The relative amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium
The time taken for a reaction to reach equilibrium from its starting point
The point at which the forward reaction stops and the reverse begins
The temperature at which the forward and reverse rates become equal
questions.explanation: An equilibrium lying 'to the right' has a high proportion of products; one lying 'to the left' has mostly reactants. The time taken depends on the rate, not the position.

questions.stem: Hydrogen and iodine are mixed in a sealed flask: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). How do the forward and reverse rates change from the moment of mixing until equilibrium?
options: Both rates fall steadily until both reactions stop at equilibrium
Both rates stay constant, but the forward rate is always greater
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal
The forward rate rises and the reverse rate falls until they are equal
questions.explanation: At first there is no HI, so the reverse rate is zero and the forward rate is at its highest. As H₂ and I₂ are used up the forward rate falls, and as HI builds up the reverse rate rises, until they are equal.

questions.stem: For a reaction, the forward activation energy is 120 kJ/mol and ΔH = -80 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
options: -200 kJ/mol
200 kJ/mol
40 kJ/mol
120 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: For an exothermic reaction the products are lower in energy, so the reverse reaction must climb the whole barrier: Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) + 80 = 200 kJ/mol. Subtracting gives 40 kJ/mol, which would be true for an endothermic reaction.

questions.stem: Why is the combustion of methane not reversible in practice, while the reaction N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is easily reversed?
options: Combustion has a very high forward activation energy, so the products cannot form at all
N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is strongly exothermic, so both directions have very low activation energies
Combustion takes place in an open system, so its products never collide with each other
Combustion is so exothermic that its reverse activation energy is far too high
questions.explanation: Combustion releases a great deal of energy, so the reverse reaction has an enormous activation energy and almost never occurs. In N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ both activation energies are small, so both directions proceed at room temperature.

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = -92 kJ/mol. What happens to the equilibrium yield of ammonia when temperature is increased?
options: It increases, because all reactions go faster at higher temperature
It increases, because the exothermic forward reaction is favoured
It is unchanged, because temperature affects only the reaction rate
It decreases, because the endothermic reverse reaction is favoured
questions.explanation: Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, which absorbs the added heat; here that is the reverse reaction, so less ammonia is present at equilibrium. Both rates increase, but the reverse rate increases more.

questions.stem: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of the endothermic direction of an equilibrium more than the exothermic direction?
options: The endothermic direction has fewer particles, so its collisions increase more as particles speed up
Heat is a reactant in the exothermic direction, so adding heat slows that direction down
The endothermic direction has the higher activation energy, so it is more temperature sensitive
The exothermic direction has the higher activation energy, so its rate falls as temperature rises
questions.explanation: The endothermic direction has the larger activation energy; a rise in temperature increases the fraction of particles with that energy proportionally more. Both rates increase, so the exothermic rate does not fall.

questions.stem: 2NO₂(g, brown) ⇌ N₂O₄(g, colourless), ΔH negative. A sealed tube of the mixture is placed in ice water. What colour change is seen?
options: It becomes paler, because the exothermic forward reaction is favoured
The mixture becomes darker brown, because the reverse reaction is favoured
The mixture becomes colourless, because both reactions stop when cold
The colour is unchanged, because cooling affects both reactions equally
questions.explanation: Cooling favours the exothermic direction, which releases heat; here that converts brown NO₂ to colourless N₂O₄, so the mixture becomes paler. Heating has the opposite effect.

questions.stem: [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺(aq, pink) + 4Cl⁻(aq) ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻(aq, blue) + 6H₂O(l). A pink solution turns blue when heated. What can be deduced?
options: Heating has removed the chloride ions
Heating has acted as a catalyst
The forward reaction is endothermic
The forward reaction is exothermic
questions.explanation: Heating shifts an equilibrium in the endothermic direction. The shift towards blue [CoCl₄]²⁻ shows the forward reaction is endothermic. A catalyst does not shift equilibrium position.

questions.stem: In the cobalt chloride equilibrium, concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to the pink solution and it turns blue. How does collision theory explain this?
options: More chloride ions increase the frequency of forward collisions, so the forward rate exceeds the reverse
More chloride ions increase the frequency of reverse collisions, so the reverse rate exceeds the forward
The acid raises the temperature, so the endothermic reverse reaction becomes the faster reaction
The acid lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction, so only the forward reaction occurs
questions.explanation: Adding a reactant raises its concentration, so forward collisions become more frequent. The forward rate briefly exceeds the reverse rate, more blue product forms, and a new equilibrium is reached.

questions.stem: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), what is the effect of increasing the pressure by decreasing the volume?
options: The equilibrium shifts right, towards the side with fewer gas particles
The equilibrium shifts left, towards the side with more gas particles
The equilibrium does not shift, because all the species are gases
The equilibrium shifts left, because pressure always favours reactants
questions.explanation: There are 3 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. Decreasing the volume raises all concentrations, but collisions in the forward direction (more particles) increase more, so the equilibrium shifts right.

questions.stem: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the volume of the container is halved at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
options: The position shifts right, because the pressure increase raises the value of K
The position does not change, because both sides have the same number of gas particles
The position shifts right, because a smaller volume always favours the products
The position shifts left, because a smaller volume favours the side with diatomic molecules
questions.explanation: Two moles of gas are on each side, so halving the volume raises forward and reverse rates equally and the position is unchanged, although all concentrations double. K changes only with temperature.

questions.stem: Argon is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ in a rigid container of fixed volume. What happens to the equilibrium position?
options: It shifts right, because the total pressure in the container has increased
It shifts left, because argon reacts with some of the ammonia present
It shifts right, because argon collides with nitrogen and speeds it up
Nothing, because the concentrations of the reacting gases are unchanged
questions.explanation: Total pressure rises, but at fixed volume the concentrations of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ do not change, so the forward and reverse rates are unaffected. Argon is unreactive.

questions.stem: What is the effect of adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium?
options: No change in position, because both rates increase equally
The equilibrium shifts right, because the forward reaction is sped up
The equilibrium shifts left, because the reverse reaction is sped up
The value of K increases, because the activation energy is lowered
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both directions by the same amount, so both rates increase equally. Equilibrium is reached sooner but its position and K are unchanged.

questions.stem: What does Le Chatelier's principle state?
options: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to make the change even larger
A system at equilibrium cannot be disturbed by changes in conditions
A disturbed system returns exactly to its original concentrations
A disturbed equilibrium shifts so as to partly counteract the change
questions.explanation: The system responds by favouring the direction that reduces the effect of the change. It does not fully undo the change, so the new equilibrium differs from the old one.

questions.stem: In the equilibrium N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ammonia is removed from the mixture as it forms. What happens, and why is this done industrially?
options: The equilibrium shifts left to replace nitrogen, so the reaction must be restarted
The reaction stops, because no ammonia remains to take part in the reverse reaction
The value of K increases, so a larger proportion of ammonia forms at equilibrium
The equilibrium keeps shifting right to replace ammonia, increasing the overall yield
questions.explanation: Removing a product lowers its concentration, so the reverse rate falls and the forward reaction is favoured. Continually removing ammonia drives more conversion of reactants. K is unchanged.

questions.stem: For an exothermic gas reaction with fewer moles of gas on the product side, which set of conditions gives the highest equilibrium yield?
options: Low temperature and low pressure
High temperature and low pressure
Low temperature and high pressure
High temperature and high pressure
questions.explanation: Low temperature favours the exothermic direction and high pressure favours the side with fewer gas particles, so both favour products. Industry often uses a moderate temperature with a catalyst because low temperatures make the rate too slow.

questions.stem: Why does the industrial production of ammonia use a moderate temperature rather than a low one, even though low temperature favours a higher yield?
options: At low temperature the reverse reaction is favoured, so very little ammonia forms
At low temperature the iron catalyst works faster, which damages the equipment
At low temperature nitrogen becomes a liquid, so it cannot react with hydrogen
At low temperature the rate is too slow, so rate and yield are balanced
questions.explanation: A lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield but reaches equilibrium far too slowly. A moderate temperature with a catalyst gives an acceptable yield at a useful rate.

questions.stem: What is the equilibrium constant expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
options: K = [N₂][H₂]³ / [NH₃]²
K = 2[NH₃] / ([N₂] x 3[H₂])
K = [NH₃] / ([N₂][H₂])
K = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³)
questions.explanation: Products go on top and reactants underneath, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Coefficients are powers, not multipliers.

questions.stem: One reaction has K = 1 x 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What does this indicate?
options: The reaction has stopped completely at equilibrium
At equilibrium the mixture is mostly reactants
At equilibrium the mixture is mostly products
The reaction reaches equilibrium very slowly
questions.explanation: A very small K means the denominator (reactants) is far larger than the numerator (products), so the equilibrium lies well to the left. K says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

questions.stem: For A(g) + B(g) ⇌ C(g), K = 4.0 at a certain temperature. A mixture has [A] = 1.0 mol/L, [B] = 2.0 mol/L and [C] = 2.0 mol/L. What will happen?
options: Net reverse reaction, because the concentration ratio (1.0) is less than K
No change, because the mixture contains equal amounts of B and C
Net reverse reaction, because there is more B than A in the mixture
Net forward reaction, because the concentration ratio (1.0) is less than K
questions.explanation: The reaction quotient is [C] / ([A][B]) = 2.0 / (1.0 x 2.0) = 1.0. Since this is less than K, more product must form to reach equilibrium, so there is a net forward reaction.

questions.stem: Which change alters the value of the equilibrium constant for a reaction?
options: Changing the temperature
Adding more of a reactant
Adding a suitable catalyst
Decreasing the volume
questions.explanation: K depends only on temperature. Changing concentration or volume shifts the position, but the system adjusts until the concentration ratio again equals the same K; a catalyst changes neither.

questions.stem: For an exothermic reaction, how does the value of K change as temperature increases?
options: It increases, because the equilibrium shifts towards the products
It is unchanged, because K depends only on concentrations
It increases, because both reactions become faster at higher temperature
It decreases, because the equilibrium shifts towards the reactants
questions.explanation: Heating favours the endothermic reverse reaction, so at the new equilibrium there are fewer products and more reactants, and K is smaller. Faster rates alone do not change K.

questions.stem: The reaction 2X ⇌ Y has K = 50 at a certain temperature. What is K for the reverse reaction, Y ⇌ 2X, at the same temperature?
questions.explanation: Writing the reaction in reverse turns the expression upside down, so K(reverse) = 1 / 50 = 0.020. Squaring gives 2500, which is the change for doubling the coefficients.

questions.stem: A sealed bottle of soft drink shows no bubbles, but when the cap is removed it fizzes. Which statement explains this?
options: Opening adds oxygen to the bottle, which reacts with the dissolved CO₂ to form bubbles
Opening raises the temperature of the drink, which makes all of the CO₂ boil at once
Opening makes it an open system, so CO₂ gas escapes and more CO₂ leaves the solution
Opening makes it a closed system, so CO₂ gas builds up above the drink and bubbles out
questions.explanation: In the sealed bottle CO₂(aq) ⇌ CO₂(g) is at equilibrium. Once opened, gaseous CO₂ escapes, so dissolved CO₂ keeps coming out of solution as bubbles and equilibrium cannot be re-established.

questions.stem: Which of these systems can reach a state of equilibrium?
options: Magnesium dissolving in an open beaker of acid
Water and its vapour in a sealed flask
Water evaporating from an open dish
Petrol burning in a car engine
questions.explanation: Equilibrium needs a closed system, so that products can react back or condense. In an open dish the vapour escapes, and burning fuel or magnesium releasing hydrogen gas into the air go to completion.

questions.stem: For an endothermic reaction, the forward activation energy is 150 kJ/mol and ΔH = +50 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?
options: 100 kJ/mol
200 kJ/mol
50 kJ/mol
-100 kJ/mol
questions.explanation: For an endothermic reaction the products are higher in energy than the reactants, so the reverse barrier is smaller: 150 - 50 = 100 kJ/mol. Adding the two gives 200 kJ/mol, which would apply to an exothermic reaction.

questions.stem: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq, deep red). A few drops of concentrated Fe³⁺ solution are added to the equilibrium mixture. What is observed?
options: The colour does not change, because K stays the same
The solution goes colourless as SCN⁻ is used up
The solution becomes a deeper red as more FeSCN²⁺ forms
The solution becomes paler as FeSCN²⁺ breaks down
questions.explanation: Adding a reactant increases the frequency of forward collisions, so the forward rate briefly exceeds the reverse rate and more red FeSCN²⁺ forms. K is unchanged, but the position shifts right.

questions.stem: The same Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) equilibrium mixture is diluted by adding a large volume of water. Which way does the position shift, and why?
options: Left, because dilution lowers the forward collision rate (two reacting particles) more than the reverse
Right, because dilution lowers the reverse collision rate (one particle) more than the forward
Neither way, because water does not appear in the equation for the equilibrium
Right, because the added water reacts with Fe³⁺ ions to form more FeSCN²⁺ ions
questions.explanation: Diluting lowers every concentration. The forward reaction needs two particles to collide, so its rate falls more than that of the reverse reaction, which involves one; the position shifts towards the side with more dissolved particles.

questions.stem: 2CrO₄²⁻(aq, yellow) + 2H⁺(aq) ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq, orange) + H₂O(l). Sodium hydroxide solution is added to the orange mixture. What happens?
options: It turns a deeper orange, because OH⁻ adds to the dichromate ions present
It turns yellow, because NaOH lowers the temperature of the mixture
Nothing happens, because H⁺ is only a catalyst in this equilibrium
It turns yellow, because OH⁻ removes H⁺ and the reverse reaction is favoured
questions.explanation: Hydroxide ions react with hydrogen ions to form water, lowering [H⁺]. The forward rate falls, so the reverse reaction is favoured and more yellow chromate forms. Adding acid has the opposite effect.

questions.stem: A graph shows the concentrations of N₂, H₂ and NH₃ in an equilibrium mixture at constant temperature. At one moment the H₂ concentration jumps up, then all three concentrations change gradually to new constant values. What happened?
options: Hydrogen was added, and the system shifted right, using up some H₂ and N₂
The temperature was raised, and the system shifted left to absorb the heat
A catalyst was added, and all the concentrations moved towards equal values
The volume was increased, and every concentration rose at the same moment
questions.explanation: A sudden rise in only one species shows it was added. The forward reaction is then favoured, so H₂ and N₂ fall gradually while NH₃ rises. A temperature change causes gradual changes with no sudden jump, and a catalyst does not shift the position.

questions.stem: A reaction mixture is at equilibrium. At time t, extra reactant is added. Which describes how the forward and reverse rates change from time t until equilibrium is restored?
options: The forward rate jumps then falls, the reverse rate rises, and they become equal again
The forward rate falls then rises, the reverse rate stays constant, and they become equal
Both rates jump up at once and stay at the new values, so the position does not change
The reverse rate jumps then falls, the forward rate rises, and they become equal again
questions.explanation: Extra reactant immediately increases forward collisions, so the forward rate jumps. As reactant is used and product forms, the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they are equal at a new equilibrium.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 1 x 10¹² at 25 °C. What can be concluded about the equilibrium mixture?
options: It contains mostly products, so the reaction goes almost to completion
It contains mostly reactants, so the reaction barely proceeds at all
It contains equal amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium
It forms very quickly, because a large K means a fast reaction
questions.explanation: A very large K means the products in the numerator greatly outweigh the reactants, so the position lies far to the right. K tells us nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.
